finding: The live range is a little too low at both ends rather than wrong: the bottom is too low and the top is slightly short. Our implied totals per front wheel (parts + hours x $120-$160/hr) are: economy 2015 Corolla (press-in bearing) $256-$724; midsize 2016 Camry (press-in bearing) $267-$784; truck 2016 F-150 4WD (bolt-on hub) $459-$775; luxury 2015 BMW 328i (bolt-on hub) $354-$775. Nothing we could build gets down to $200 (the cheapest case is a $40 bearing plus 1.8 hours), and the lowest benchmark figures are about $346-$361, so $200 understates the floor by roughly $50-$150. At the top, OEM parts push three of four classes to about $775-$785, and RepairPal shows $648-$812 for a 2016 F-150 hub, so $700 clips real quotes. A range of roughly $250-$800 fits the evidence better. The two designs cost about the same in total for different reasons: press-in bearings are cheap parts with more labor, bolt-on hub assemblies are quick labor with a dearer part. Caveat: a vehicle-specific stated labor time was found only for the F-150 (Ford TSB warranty times, which also include IWE work); the Corolla, Camry and BMW hours come from general design-type times (press-in vs bolt-on), so those hour ranges are wide and less certain. A 2WD F-150 hub is far cheaper ($84.99 aftermarket) than the 4WD part used here.
extras: Quotes often add: a noise/road-test diagnosis fee; a wheel alignment after press-in bearing work where the knuckle or strut is unbolted; a new axle nut and hub mounting bolts (BMW and Ford call for new bolts); a new hub if the old one is damaged coming out of a press-in bearing (Toyota OEM hub about $178-$188 list); the ABS/wheel-speed sensor if it seizes and breaks; extra labor for rust-seized hubs (the Detroit Axle guide cites 30-90 more minutes); doing both sides of the axle; shop supplies and sales tax.
